skip_reason: Not a sales call — existing customer service. Melissa Betts already had two moves booked (a storage-to-storage move moved to Friday and a house-to-storage move set for tomorrow) and called because her storage facility's elevator is still broken. The entire call is rescheduling/consolidation: Amy cancels the storage-to-storage move, moves tomorrow's move to Friday 8/28 in a 12:30–2:30 window, and sends a confirmation plus a cancellation email. No new lead, no quote build, no booking of new business — the one price mentioned ($1,115 for 5.5 hours) was a re-estimate of an already-booked job with stairs added. The 85-pt sales rubric does not apply.
top_strength: Amy untangled a genuinely confusing two-booking situation without making the customer repeat herself, correctly caught and updated a wrong data point in the profile (storage unit was on the 2nd floor, not the 5th), and proactively re-estimated the time and cost impact of losing the elevator before the customer had to ask.
coaching_note: N/A for sales scoring, but the one real miss: Melissa's whole call was driven by damage anxiety ('I use a different set of movers last time and they broke a lot of my stuff... that insurance doesn't cover anything in real life'). Amy responded with wrap and blankets but never named No Worries Damage Coverage — up to $2,000 to repair, replace, or reimburse — which is the exact answer to the objection she raised. On service calls with a damage-worried customer, say the coverage by name and the dollar figure.
phone_presence_notes: Warm, patient, and validating throughout ('That makes sense. No worries, I understand your concern about the damages', 'That's very generous and thoughtful of you, thank you so much Melissa'), and the customer closed with 'I feel very confident' and 'thank you for making that transition easy.'
